item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #449
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property market has seen significant developments this week, with issues ranging from rising tenancy fraud to increased Right to Buy sales and proposals for stricter penalties for landlords. These changes could have far-reaching implications for homeowners, tenants, and property investors alike.

AI-Driven Tenancy Fraud on the Rise

Recent research by Goodlord has highlighted a worrying trend in the rental market: fraudulent tenancy applications are becoming increasingly sophisticated, costing landlords and letting agents an average of £9,600 per tenancy. Scammers are using artificial intelligence to create convincing fake documents, such as bank statements, employment references, and IDs, making it harder for landlords to verify tenant information. Over the past year, tenancy fraud has surged by 40%, with the overall cost to the industry now estimated at £4.1 billion annually.

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has urged landlords to remain vigilant, describing the report as a "wake-up call" for the sector. With fraudsters becoming more adept at exploiting technology, property owners might consider implementing stricter verification processes to mitigate risks.

Right to Buy Sales Surge

Government data has revealed a significant increase in Right to Buy sales, with 14,275 council homes sold in England during 2025-26. This marks a 90% rise compared to the previous year, potentially driven by tenants rushing to take advantage of the scheme before new rules come into effect. These changes will extend the minimum eligibility period and reduce the discounts available to buyers.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, has raised concerns about the impact of these sales on the wider housing market. With social housing stock dwindling, the need for replacement homes has become increasingly urgent. The Resolution Foundation reports that 1.3 million households are currently on local authority waiting lists, the highest number since 2014. Many low-income families are left with no choice but to rent more expensive private accommodation, exacerbating the housing crisis.

Proposed Fines for Landlords

Local authorities are also considering stricter enforcement measures for landlords. For instance, Bath & North East Somerset Council has proposed heavy fines for property owners who fail to meet regulatory standards. However, councils must adhere to their enforcement policies and cannot impose penalties arbitrarily. These measures aim to improve housing conditions and protect tenants, but they could also place additional financial burdens on landlords.

As the property market continues to evolve, homeowners, tenants, and landlords alike may need to stay informed about these developments. From tackling tenancy fraud to addressing housing shortages, the challenges facing the sector are complex and multifaceted. Keeping abreast of these changes could help individuals make informed decisions in an increasingly unpredictable market.

item.title: The Property Upgrades Tenants Notice Most When Viewing a Rental Home
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With the UK rental market more competitive than ever, landlords seeking to attract quality tenants might consider targeted property upgrades that maximise appeal during viewings. Research suggests certain improvements significantly influence tenant decisions, potentially reducing void periods and supporting stronger rental yields. So which features do renters prioritise?

First Impressions: Curb Appeal & Cleanliness

Tenants often form opinions within seconds of arriving, making exterior presentation crucial. Simple upgrades like repainting the front door, ensuring clear pathways, and maintaining tidy landscaping can create an instant positive impression. Inside, cleanliness reigns supreme – professional deep cleaning, fresh grout in bathrooms, and odour-neutralising treatments signal a well-maintained property.

Landlords may wish to focus on:

  • Neutral, freshly painted walls (magnolia remains a safe choice)
  • Sparkling kitchen appliances and spotless worktops
  • Bathroom fixtures free from limescale or mildew

Practical Upgrades That Add Value

Beyond aesthetics, renters frequently prioritise functional improvements that enhance daily living. Energy efficiency features like double glazing and modern boilers increasingly influence tenant decisions amidst rising utility costs. Storage solutions also rank highly – built-in wardrobes or clever under-stair cupboards can make compact spaces feel more liveable.

Other worthwhile considerations include:

  • USB charging points near beds and sofas
  • Ample, well-placed lighting (particularly in darker rooms)
  • Quality flooring that withstands wear and tear

Whilst major renovations may not always be cost-effective, small touches like replacing dated light fittings or installing a water-efficient showerhead could make a property stand out from comparable rentals.

The Kitchen: A Key Deciding Factor

Many letting agents report that kitchens disproportionately influence tenant choices. Rather than full replacements, landlords might consider cost-effective refreshes like replacing cracked tiles, updating cabinet handles, or regrouting work surfaces. Ensuring appliances are in good working order is essential – tenants often test taps, ovens and extractor fans during viewings.

The rental market shows no signs of slowing, meaning strategic investments in property presentation could prove valuable for landlords aiming to secure dependable, long-term tenants. By focusing on upgrades that genuinely matter to renters, property owners may achieve better returns without undertaking prohibitively expensive renovations.

item.title: Unfreezing housing benefits will not drive up rents
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research challenges the assumption that increasing housing benefit payments would automatically push up private rental prices across the UK. As the government considers whether to extend the current freeze on Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates beyond April 2025, analysis from the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) suggests no direct correlation between benefit levels and rent inflation.

The impact of frozen housing benefits

LHA rates, which determine how much housing benefit private renters can claim, were originally designed to cover the lowest 50% of local market rents when introduced in 2008. Following cuts in 2011, this was reduced to the bottom 30% of rents. The current freeze means fewer than 2% of private rentals remain affordable for benefit recipients, according to homelessness charity Crisis.

Historical data reveals an interesting pattern: between 2008-2016 when LHA rates rose annually with rents, average weekly rents increased by 2.5% per year. However, during the 2016-2024 period when rates were mostly frozen, rents actually rose faster at 3.4% annually. This suggests other market factors may have greater influence on rental prices than benefit levels.

Potential benefits of adjusting LHA rates

Experts highlight several advantages to realigning housing support with current market rents. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates maintaining LHA at the 30th percentile would cost £1.5bn annually - significantly less than the £2.8bn councils spent on temporary accommodation last year.

Research from the Resolution Foundation indicates that restoring LHA rates could have substantial social benefits:

  • Covering the lowest 30% of rents might lift 75,000 children and 125,000 adults out of poverty
  • Returning to the original 50th percentile could help 130,000 children and 215,000 adults escape poverty

With approximately one quarter of private renters receiving housing support, the current freeze has created significant affordability challenges across many regions. The IFS has cautioned that fiscal constraints shouldn't justify a system that creates uncertainty for renters and regional inequalities.

As the debate continues, housing advocates argue that evidence increasingly shows maintaining frozen benefit rates may be doing little to control rents while exacerbating housing insecurity for vulnerable tenants. The government faces difficult choices balancing welfare spending with ensuring adequate housing support.

item.title: Air-conditioning searches double as 61% consider installation
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As Britain experiences increasingly warm summers, new data suggests homeowners are prioritising cooling features when searching for properties. Rightmove reports a 104% surge in searches for homes with air conditioning compared to last summer, while over 60% of households now contemplate installing cooling systems.

Heatwaves reshaping property priorities

Recent Rightmove research surveying 1,062 adults reveals only 11% find their homes remain comfortable during heatwaves, with 45% struggling to maintain cool temperatures indoors. This shift in climate awareness appears to be influencing housing decisions, with 87% of respondents considering a property's summer cooling capabilities important when moving home.

Property expert Colleen Babcock notes: "Whilst location and affordability remain fundamental factors, we're seeing buyers pay closer attention to how homes perform in warmer weather. The market is responding to this growing demand, with more prospective buyers actively searching for properties featuring built-in cooling solutions."

Homeowners adapt to rising temperatures

Many households are already implementing practical measures to combat summer heat:

  • 56% have installed improved window coverings like blackout blinds or reflective film
  • 48% use fans as their primary cooling method
  • 38% have upgraded insulation to regulate indoor temperatures
  • 29% have added garden shading through trees or structures

Estate agents report growing interest in energy-efficient cooling solutions. Mark Wiggin of Mark Wiggin Estate Agents observes: "We're seeing heightened demand for properties with air source heat pumps, solar panels and integrated air conditioning systems. International buyers often expect these features as standard, and UK buyers are increasingly following suit."

Whilst only 12% of homeowners currently have air conditioning installed, 61% would consider adding it. Other popular considerations include external shading (58%) and improved ventilation systems (52%). These trends suggest that Britain's changing climate may permanently alter what buyers look for in residential properties.

As summer temperatures continue to rise, both homebuyers and existing homeowners appear to be re-evaluating their priorities. From search behaviour to renovation plans, staying cool has become a significant factor in Britain's housing market.

item.title: Scotland’s housing emergency decades in the making
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Scotland’s housing crisis has been decades in the making, according to a recent analysis by Scottish property firm DJ Alexander Ltd. The lettings and estate agency highlighted that a significant decline in social housing, combined with a growing population over the past 20 years, has culminated in the current emergency. Between 2007 and 2024, Scotland’s population increased by 402,700, while the number of occupied dwellings rose by just 286,142. This disparity has placed immense pressure on the housing market, with social housing availability shrinking by 20,267 properties during the same period.

The Shift in Housing Dynamics

Over the last two decades, there has been a notable shift in household demographics in Scotland. Smaller households, consisting of one or two people, have become increasingly common, while the prevalence of larger families has diminished. This change has necessitated a greater volume of homes to accommodate the population, yet the rate of property construction has failed to keep pace with demand. David Alexander, CEO of DJ Alexander Scotland, emphasised that the housing emergency is not a sudden development but a consequence of long-term trends. He noted, "Far too little social housing has been built, and the population continues to grow, with more people living alone or as couples. This has created a significant shortfall in housing supply."

The Role of the Private Rented Sector

While social housing has declined, the private rented sector (PRS) has played a crucial role in meeting housing demand. Over the past 20 years, the number of homes in the PRS has increased by 43.4%, now totalling 107,242 more properties than in 2007. This growth has helped to mitigate the lack of available social housing, providing much-needed accommodation for many. Alexander pointed out, "Without landlords and property investors, the housing shortage would have been far more severe. The private rented sector has filled a gap that the social sector has been unable to address."

Despite the rise in PRS properties, challenges remain. Homeownership has seen a slight decline in percentage terms, falling from 62% in 2007 to 60% in 2024. However, the actual number of homeowners has reached a record high of 1,645,318, reflecting an increase of nearly 100,000 over the past five years. This highlights the complex dynamics of Scotland’s housing market, where multiple sectors are struggling to meet the diverse needs of the population.

As Scotland’s housing crisis continues to unfold, it underscores the urgent need for a comprehensive strategy to address the shortfall in social housing and ensure that supply meets demand. With population growth showing no signs of slowing, the issue remains a pressing concern for policymakers and stakeholders alike.

item.title: Landlords lodge almost 29,000 possession claims
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data reveals that landlords in England and Wales lodged 28,610 possession claims between April 2025 and March 2026, highlighting the ongoing complexities within the rental market. Despite high tenant demand, soaring rents, and fierce competition for properties, court proceedings remain a significant aspect of landlord-tenant relationships. These claims often stem from issues such as rent arrears, breaches of tenancy agreements, or antisocial behaviour, though they do not always result in evictions or possession orders.

Regional Breakdown of Possession Claims

London accounted for the highest number of possession claims, with 10,186 cases representing nearly 36% of the total across England and Wales. The South East followed with 3,396 claims, while the North West and West Midlands recorded 3,255 and 2,402 claims respectively. At a local authority level, Newham topped the list with 984 claims, followed by Birmingham (691), Redbridge (615), Enfield (588), and Croydon (544). Other areas featuring prominently included Barking and Dagenham, Lewisham, Ealing, Manchester, and Greenwich.

The Challenges for Landlords

Even in a competitive rental market, landlords may face prolonged periods without rental income whilst navigating possession claims. The process has become increasingly regulated, emphasising the importance of accurate documentation, evidence, and legal guidance. Sim Sekhon, Group CEO of LegalforLandlords, noted that while high demand often paints landlords as holding the upper hand, the reality is far more nuanced. He explained that tenancies can still break down despite strong demand, and landlords may need to recover possession when serious issues arise.

Sekhon added, "Good landlords aim for successful, long-term tenancies. However, when possession becomes unavoidable, having access to experienced legal support is crucial to ensure the process is handled correctly. Mistakes can lead to delays, additional costs, and prolonged financial losses."

These figures underscore the delicate balance landlords must strike between maintaining profitable tenancies and addressing unavoidable disputes. For those navigating the rental market, understanding both rights and responsibilities remains essential.

item.title: Housing demand and sales are stagnant, says RICS
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market remains in a holding pattern, with buyer demand and completed sales showing little movement in July, according to the latest RICS Residential Market Survey. The report suggests ongoing economic uncertainties and mortgage affordability challenges continue to dampen market activity across most regions.

Market activity remains subdued

New buyer enquiries recorded a net balance of -28% in July, unchanged from June's figure. While this represents an improvement from March's low of -41%, it indicates demand remains significantly weaker than historical averages. Similarly, agreed sales held steady at -30%, mirroring June's results but showing some recovery from April's -37% reading.

Regional variations paint an uneven picture, with London, the South East and South West experiencing more pronounced price declines than the national average. Northern Ireland continues to buck the trend with rising prices, while Scotland's previously strong growth appears to be stabilising.

Price expectations reflect caution

Short-term price projections remain pessimistic, with a three-month outlook of -31%. The twelve-month forecast sits slightly more positive at +4%, though London stands out with particularly weak expectations at -23% - a notable drop from -10% in the previous survey.

Simon Rubinsohn, RICS Chief Economist, noted: "The combination of geopolitical tensions, domestic political uncertainty and mortgage affordability challenges continues to weigh on market sentiment. The subdued forward-looking indicators suggest this cautious climate may persist."

Louise Apollonio of Shawbrook added: "The typical summer uplift in activity hasn't materialised this year. Various factors including extreme weather, political changes and broader economic concerns appear to be causing many potential buyers to adopt a wait-and-see approach."

Looking ahead

Market observers suggest the upcoming Autumn Budget on 28th October could influence buyer behaviour, with some households potentially delaying decisions until the government's fiscal plans become clearer. The persistent cost-of-living pressures and mortgage rate volatility mean any significant market recovery may need to wait until 2024.

For those considering entering the market, comparing mortgage deals and seeking independent financial advice could help navigate the current climate. However, with price expectations varying significantly by region, local market research remains essential.

item.title: Another day, another PM, another Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market has long been a cornerstone of the nation’s economy, yet its potential is often hindered by political uncertainty and shifting fiscal policies. Historically, Budget announcements were made in March or April, allowing homeowners to prepare for the prime selling season. However, since 2017, the main Budget has been moved to late autumn, coinciding with a period of heightened political volatility. This shift has created apprehension among buyers, sellers, and investors, dampening what is traditionally the second-best period for property transactions.

The Impact of Political Instability

Over the past decade, the UK has experienced significant political upheaval, with frequent changes in leadership and policy direction. This instability has made it challenging for the property market to thrive, as uncertainty often leads to hesitation among buyers and sellers. The five-year political cycle, intended to provide stability, has been disrupted by early elections and shifting ideologies. As a result, long-term economic planning has become increasingly difficult, leaving the property sector without a cohesive strategy.

Unlike countries such as China, where a one-party system allows for consistent long-term planning, the UK’s political landscape is marked by frequent changes in leadership and policy. This unpredictability has discouraged private investment in property, as investors are wary of sudden shifts in taxation or regulation. With UK Property PLC accounting for around 10% of the nation’s economy, the lack of a coherent plan for the sector could have far-reaching consequences.

Proposing a Solution

To mitigate the impact of political uncertainty, some experts have suggested creating a council of property professionals to guide policy decisions. This council could include individuals with extensive experience in the property market, planning processes, and commercial imperatives. By leveraging their expertise, it may be possible to develop policies that support long-term investment and address the diverse needs of different regions and demographics.

Local mayoral input could also play a role in shaping property policy, ensuring that decisions reflect the unique challenges and opportunities of each area. However, detailed proposals for such a scheme are still lacking. Despite this, there is no shortage of experienced property professionals who are eager to contribute to solutions that benefit both homeowners and investors.

item.title: Reaction to UK Finance mortgage arrears data
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data from UK Finance reveals positive trends in mortgage arrears and possessions across both residential and buy-to-let sectors during the second quarter of 2026. The figures highlight lenders' ongoing commitment to supporting borrowers facing financial challenges, with notable quarterly improvements particularly evident in the rental property market.

Arrears show downward trend

The latest statistics indicate that 77,940 homeowner mortgages were in arrears of 2.5% or more of their outstanding balance during Q2 2026 – a modest 1% reduction compared to the previous quarter. The decline was more pronounced in the buy-to-let sector, where 8,390 BTL mortgages fell into this arrears category, marking a 6% quarterly improvement.

Industry experts suggest these reductions reflect both the effectiveness of lender support schemes and the gradual easing of broader economic pressures. However, commentators caution that affordability challenges persist for many households, emphasising the importance of early engagement with lenders when financial difficulties arise.

Possessions remain below historic averages

Repossession figures continue to show encouraging signs, remaining substantially lower than long-term historical averages. During Q2 2026, 1,150 residential properties were taken into possession – an 8% quarterly decrease and 14% annual reduction. The buy-to-let market saw more significant progress, with just 630 rental properties repossessed, representing a 22% quarterly decline and 20% annual improvement.

James Tatch, head of analytics at UK Finance, noted that this marks the first year-on-year decrease in possessions since late 2023. He reiterated that lenders maintain comprehensive support options for borrowers concerned about meeting repayments, with tailored assistance available through early dialogue.

Market stakeholders emphasise proactive approach

Property professionals have welcomed the positive trends while highlighting ongoing challenges in the housing market. NAEA Propertymark President Ian Harris pointed out that most current possessions relate to older mortgages, underlining the importance of continued collaboration between lenders, agents and policymakers to support at-risk borrowers.

Harris particularly emphasised the need for landlords to seek early advice when facing financial pressure, as rental property difficulties can have wider implications for housing availability. The property industry continues to advocate for preventative measures and early intervention strategies to help maintain market stability.

For homeowners or landlords experiencing repayment concerns, financial institutions recommend making contact at the earliest opportunity. Most lenders offer various support options, including temporary payment reductions, term extensions or switching to interest-only arrangements, with solutions tailored to individual circumstances.

item.title: Landlords ‘raising asking rents as bidding war ban hits’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Following the introduction of Labour’s Renters’ Rights Act, landlords across the UK have been increasing their asking rents, according to recent reports. While this may seem counterintuitive, the trend appears to be linked to the Act’s ban on competitive bidding for rental properties. Letting agents and landlords are no longer permitted to encourage tenants to bid against one another, prompting many to set higher initial asking prices in anticipation of negotiations.

Impact of the Renters’ Rights Act

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced in May, initially brought a surge of activity to the rental market as landlords and tenants adjusted to the new rules. However, Chestertons, a leading estate agency, noted that this activity stabilised by July. The legislation’s prohibition on bidding wars has led landlords to adopt a different strategy. By setting higher asking rents, landlords aim to secure offers closer to their desired price, even if tenants negotiate downwards.

This shift in pricing strategies is beginning to reflect in rental market data. Rightmove’s Rental Trends Tracker highlights that asking rents rose by 2.9% year-on-year during the second quarter of 2026, marking the strongest growth rate in two years. London, in particular, saw rental growth outpace the rest of the UK for the first time since late 2023, with a 2.3% increase.

Market Dynamics and Tenant Demand

The trend of higher asking rents first emerged in June and has continued into July, albeit at a slower pace. Landlords appear to be growing more confident in their pricing strategies, particularly as supply levels in the rental market remain constrained. Many landlords are either selling properties or reducing their portfolios, while tenant demand continues to rise.

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, commented on the evolving market dynamics: “Activity seen immediately after the legislation was introduced in May eased off in July. However, in the first 10 days of August, our branches have seen applicant registrations up 18% year-on-year, which aligns with the seasonal summer uptick we would expect at this time of year.”

This combination of reduced supply and increased demand is likely to sustain upward pressure on rental prices in the coming months. Prospective tenants may wish to act swiftly to secure rental properties, particularly in high-demand areas like London.

As the rental market continues to adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act, both landlords and tenants will need to navigate these changes carefully. Landlords might consider setting realistic asking prices, whilst tenants could benefit from being well-prepared for negotiations in a competitive market.

item.title: Homes in Glasgow sell fastest in the UK
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals striking regional variations in how quickly UK properties are snapped up by buyers, with Glasgow leading the pack as Britain's fastest-moving housing market. Homes in the Scottish city are securing sales agreements in just 11 days on average – significantly quicker than the national average of 30 days.

Regional hotspots and slow sellers

The study, drawing on data from over 6,000 estate agents, shows Worcester and Belfast joining Glasgow as the top three fastest-selling locations. At the other end of the spectrum, Wakefield properties take the longest to sell at 63 days, more than double Glasgow's speed. London sits precisely at the national average, ranking 21st among the cities analysed.

Property type also plays a crucial role in selling speed. Terraced and semi-detached homes prove most popular nationwide, typically finding buyers within 26 days. In contrast, detached properties take 41 days on average, while retirement and sheltered accommodation linger longest at 98 days. The data highlights particular challenges in the flat market, where sales times have increased by 34% year-on-year to 39 days.

Pricing strategies make the difference

Industry experts suggest Glasgow's success stems from estate agents' precise local knowledge and realistic pricing from day one. Riccardo Iannucci-Dawson of Alto, which conducted the research, notes: "The first fortnight on the market is critical – homes priced for what local buyers will actually pay move quickly, while those anchored to outdated expectations tend to stagnate."

The findings underscore how flats face particular headwinds, with one-bed and studio properties seeing a 31% increase in selling times. This trend may reflect shifting buyer priorities post-pandemic, as many purchasers prioritise space over urban convenience. The research team has created a free online tool allowing homeowners to check typical selling times in their postcode area.

For those considering selling, the data suggests regional markets remain highly varied. While Glasgow's lightning-fast sales might tempt sellers to test higher prices, the overall message is clear – accurate, locally-informed valuations from the outset typically yield better results than starting high and discounting over time. As housing demand continues to evolve, understanding these local dynamics could prove invaluable for homeowners navigating today's market.

item.title: As rental supply shrinks, where do renters compete the most?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Britain's rental market is facing intense competition across the board, with renters battling for rooms in both budget-friendly and premium locations. New data reveals surprising hotspots where demand far outstrips supply, creating challenging conditions for tenants seeking affordable accommodation.

Rental Demand Polarises Across the UK

Recent figures from flatshare platform SpareRoom highlight a divided rental landscape. At one end, Bootle in Merseyside sees over 12 prospective tenants competing for each available room, with average rents below £500 per month. At the other extreme, affluent Richmond commands rents exceeding £1,000 per room yet still experiences fierce competition.

This trend extends across the country, with key patterns emerging:

  • London commuter hotspots: Richmond, Worcester Park, Teddington, Morden and Ware
  • Manchester satellite towns: Sale, Wilmslow, Alderley Edge and Ashton-under-Lyne
  • Edinburgh's surrounding areas: Musselburgh, Balerno, Currie and Juniper Green

Other notable pressure points include West Bromwich near Birmingham (8 applicants per room) and Hamilton outside Glasgow (8.1 applicants per room). What unites these locations is their proximity to major employment centres while offering either affordability or desirable lifestyles.

Changing Demographics in Shared Housing

The rental squeeze reflects broader societal shifts, with SpareRoom director Matt Hutchinson observing three distinct groups driving demand:

  • Budget-conscious renters priced out of city centres
  • Young professionals extending flatsharing to accelerate savings
  • Older tenants opting for suburban shared living

Hutchinson notes: "Suburban areas often contain under-occupied homes that could help alleviate rental shortages. The government could support this by reviewing the Rent a Room Scheme threshold, which hasn't been adjusted in a decade."

With the Autumn Budget approaching, industry voices suggest updating property tax reliefs could encourage more homeowners to take in lodgers. This might help balance supply and demand while potentially slowing rental inflation across pressured markets.

For renters navigating this competitive landscape, considering commuter towns and exploring shared accommodation options could improve chances of securing suitable housing. As the market evolves, flexibility may prove as valuable as location in the search for affordable rents.

item.title: Agents need to talk says The Guild as it plans UK tour
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Guild of Property Professionals is set to embark on a UK-wide tour this autumn, aiming to foster open dialogue and collaboration among independent estate agents. Running from 7 September to 19 November, the initiative will bring together senior leaders from Guild Member offices for a series of regional meetings. Hosted by Iain McKenzie, CEO of The Guild, these gatherings will provide a platform for agents to discuss challenges, share insights, and explore opportunities in the ever-evolving property market.

Creating a Space for Collaboration

The tour, which kicks off in Exeter, will visit various locations across the country, offering agents a chance to step away from their daily routines and engage in meaningful conversations. The informal, round table format is designed to encourage participants to share their experiences, discuss what’s working in their businesses, and learn from others facing similar challenges. Unlike traditional conferences, these meetings prioritise two-way communication, allowing agents to actively contribute rather than passively listen.

McKenzie emphasised the importance of creating a supportive community where independent agents can exchange ideas and solutions. "One of the greatest strengths of The Guild is the community we’ve built around our Members," he said. "These meetings provide a space where agents can talk openly with one another, often leading to valuable insights. An agent might be dealing with an issue that another Member has already resolved, or someone could share an idea that makes a significant difference to another business."

Navigating Challenges Together

The property market is currently facing a range of pressures, from economic uncertainty and legislative changes to shifting consumer expectations and increased competition. Independent agents, in particular, may find these challenges daunting. The Guild’s regional meetings aim to address these issues by fostering a collaborative environment where agents can support one another.

"Independent agents don’t have to navigate these changes alone," McKenzie added. "Our role is to provide Members with the tools, partnerships, and opportunities they need to thrive. By coming together, agents can share knowledge and experiences that benefit the entire network."

The Guild believes that this approach not only strengthens individual businesses but also enhances the resilience of the wider property market. By encouraging honest conversations and practical support, the organisation hopes to empower agents to overcome obstacles and seize new opportunities.

As the autumn tour gets underway, The Guild of Property Professionals remains committed to building a community where independent agents can thrive. Through these regional meetings, the organisation continues to champion collaboration, innovation, and shared success in the property industry.

item.title: Void periods shorten after Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Void periods in the rental market have begun to shorten following the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act in May, according to recent research. The findings suggest that landlords are adapting to the new legislation, with average void periods across England now standing at 21 days, down from 24 days in May. While this marks a positive shift, voids remain slightly longer than the 19-day average recorded in June last year.

Regional Variations in Void Periods

Certain regions have experienced more significant improvements than others. The South West has seen the largest reduction, with void periods decreasing by 12.3 days since May. The North East followed with a 6.3-day reduction, whilst the West Midlands, North West, and Yorkshire and the Humber also recorded declines of 3.7, 2.6, and 2.3 days respectively. Despite these positive trends, some areas continue to face longer void periods compared to the previous year. For example, Yorkshire and the Humber has seen an annual increase of 3.8 days.

Landlords Adapting to New Legislation

The Renters’ Rights Act has prompted many landlords to review their practices and ensure compliance with the new regulations. Property management firm Rushbrook & Rathbone highlights that this period of change has also encouraged landlords to adopt a more professional approach to managing their portfolios. Whilst the initial focus was on meeting the Act’s requirements, there appears to be a broader shift in mindset within the private rented sector.

Roma Sharma, managing director of Rushbrook & Rathbone, commented: “It’s encouraging to see void periods beginning to reduce after what has been one of the most significant periods of change in recent years. However, landlords shouldn’t view this as a sign that the hard work is done. Continued adaptation and professionalism will be key to navigating the evolving landscape.”

As the rental market continues to adjust to the Renters’ Rights Act, landlords may wish to stay informed about regulatory changes and consider ways to enhance their property management strategies. Whilst void periods are improving, maintaining a proactive approach could help ensure long-term success in an increasingly competitive market.

item.title: Bristol still England’s Japanese knotweed capital
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Bristol has once again topped the list of England's worst Japanese knotweed hotspots, with infestation levels more than double those in any other region. New analysis by invasive plant specialists Environet reveals the city recorded 1,324 verified cases – equating to 32.29 occurrences per square mile. The findings highlight ongoing challenges for homeowners and property buyers in affected areas across the country.

Regional hotspots revealed

Merseyside ranked as the second most affected region with 13.45 knotweed sightings per square mile, followed by Greater London at 7.67 cases. Greater Manchester and Lancashire completed the top five with 7.49 and 7.00 incidences per square mile respectively. The data comes from Environet's Exposed heatmap, which compiles over 100,000 verified reports from professionals and the public.

Historical industrial areas appear particularly vulnerable, with former docklands and manufacturing centres dominating the rankings. Experts attribute this pattern to the historical movement of contaminated soil during construction projects. The research suggests about 7% of UK homes could be affected by the invasive plant – equivalent to nearly 1.58 million properties nationally.

Property market implications

Japanese knotweed can create significant complications for property transactions. Mortgage lenders often require professional treatment plans before approving loans on affected properties. Environet's research indicates infestations typically reduce property values by around 5% – representing an average £13,500 decrease on a typical UK home.

The plant's aggressive root system can cause structural damage to buildings and hard surfaces, while legal disputes may arise when it spreads across property boundaries. Homeowners may wish to check Environet's online heatmap before purchasing a property, particularly in high-risk postcodes. Professional treatment usually involves herbicide applications or physical removal of the root system.

Emily Grant, director at Environet, commented: "While southern hotspots like Bristol and London feature prominently, the north of England accounts for over half of the top 20 affected areas. Vigilance remains crucial whether buying, selling or maintaining property in these regions."

item.title: Rayner criticized over £20k speaking fee at Propertymark event
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Angela Rayner has faced criticism after accepting a £20,000 speaking fee from Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, sparking debate about political transparency during the housing affordability crisis. The payment, made for a two-hour appearance at Propertymark's June conference, has drawn attention from tenant advocacy groups questioning the influence of property industry lobbying.

Protest highlights rent control tensions

Members of the London Renters Union staged a symbolic protest outside government offices, presenting an oversized cheque for £20,001 to highlight their concerns. The group, which campaigns for stronger tenant protections, suggested the payment created a conflict of interest given Propertymark's opposition to rent controls. This comes after Rayner, upon returning as Housing Secretary in July, publicly rejected rent freezes as a solution to rising housing costs.

The Renters' Rights Act, implemented in May, introduced some protections including limiting rent increases to once annually and allowing tenants to challenge excessive rises. However, campaigners argue these measures fall short of the comprehensive rent controls they believe are needed to address the affordability crisis.

Industry defends speaker arrangements

Propertymark has defended its payment to Rayner, stating that speaker fees are standard practice for industry conferences. The organisation emphasised that Rayner was invited based on her involvement in housing policy development, particularly regarding the Renters' Rights Bill, and that she was not serving as a minister at the time of the engagement.

Nathan Emerson, Propertymark's chief executive, clarified: "There was no expectation of her returning to government when we extended the invitation. We sought her insights based on her policy experience, not her political position." The professional body has consistently opposed rent controls, arguing they could reduce investment in the private rental sector.

With housing affordability remaining a pressing issue, this incident has reignited discussions about the relationship between policymakers and industry groups. While no rules appear to have been broken, the episode highlights ongoing tensions between tenant advocates and property professionals in shaping housing policy.

item.title: Calls for clarity, new thresholds and reductions to SDLT
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The property market may see renewed activity following the Prime Minister’s swift clarification on Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) policies, according to industry experts. With political uncertainty having dampened buyer registrations in recent months, the confirmation that no abolition is planned could help stabilise market confidence.

Clarity may boost buyer confidence

Recent data from estate agency Chestertons revealed a 22% year-on-year drop in buyer registrations across London in July – the sharpest decline since last November’s pre-Budget slowdown. Adam Jennings, the firm’s head of residential, suggested that the Prime Minister’s rapid response to SDLT speculation might prevent further hesitation among prospective purchasers.

Jennings noted: “When significant sums are involved, buyers naturally tend to pause during periods of uncertainty. The immediate clarity provided by the new administration removes a key question mark for those considering property purchases.” He added that maintaining this position for the next year could give the market much-needed stability.

Frozen thresholds create affordability pressures

Meanwhile, tax specialists have highlighted how static SDLT thresholds combined with rising house prices are creating additional financial pressures. Blick Rothenberg analysis shows that whilst average UK property prices have increased by 28% over the past decade, the corresponding SDLT burden has more than doubled.

Mark Cunningham, a partner at the firm, explained: “The current system creates a growing disparity – as prices rise, more transactions fall into higher tax bands. This fiscal drag effectively reduces market mobility at a time when the government aims to boost housing supply.”

The figures reveal stark contrasts:

  • Average UK house price (2016-2026): +28.4% (£211,230 to £271,295)
  • SDLT on average-priced property: +106.7% (£1,725 to £3,565)

Cunningham suggested that without threshold adjustments, the current SDLT framework might inadvertently hinder housing market growth and the government’s construction targets.

As the property market navigates these challenges, buyers and policymakers alike may need to consider how tax structures impact housing accessibility and transaction volumes in the current economic climate.

item.title: Goodlord – do not joke about tenancy fraud
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Tenancy fraud has reached alarming levels across the UK's private rental sector, with sophisticated forgeries and fabricated identities slipping through traditional referencing checks. A recent industry report reveals this growing problem could be costing landlords and letting agents up to £4.1bn annually, while creating significant knock-on effects throughout the housing market.

The rise of AI-powered rental fraud

Modern fraudsters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing fake documents, including payslips, bank statements and employment references. These sophisticated forgeries often bypass standard verification processes, with high-value properties particularly vulnerable – approximately one in fifty applications for premium rentals now involves fraudulent activity.

The scale of the issue has grown dramatically, with referee-flagged tenancy fraud increasing by 78% year-on-year. Current fraud rates remain about 40% higher than mid-2023 levels, suggesting the problem is worsening rather than improving. Industry experts warn that the financial and administrative consequences of fraudulent tenancies extend far beyond immediate monetary losses, creating bottlenecks in an already strained housing system.

Regional variations and sector impact

Fraud rates vary significantly across the UK, with Greater London experiencing approximately double the national average. The capital remains the country's primary hotspot, followed by the West Midlands and North West. Conversely, Scotland, Wales, the North East and South West consistently report the lowest instances of tenancy fraud.

The repercussions of fraudulent applications ripple through multiple sectors:

  • Landlords face emotional stress and financial uncertainty
  • Letting agents waste valuable time processing false applications
  • Genuine tenants struggle to find available properties
  • Court systems become overloaded with possession cases

With some eviction proceedings now taking over 15 months to resolve – a timeline likely to extend under forthcoming rental reforms – the cost of inadequate tenant referencing has never been higher. Industry professionals are calling for improved verification methods and greater collaboration to combat this growing threat to the private rental sector.

As fraud techniques become more advanced, landlords and letting agents may wish to review their referencing processes and consider additional verification steps. While no system can guarantee complete protection against determined fraudsters, staying informed about current risks could help reduce exposure to this costly problem.

item.title: Affordable housing provider using AI to spot damp and mould
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Housing associations across the UK are turning to artificial intelligence to maintain property standards, with one major provider now using image recognition technology to detect damp, mould and structural issues before they escalate. Affordable housing provider Stonewater has partnered with Dutch AI specialist SPOTR to implement an innovative property management system that could transform how social housing maintenance is handled.

How AI Property Assessments Work

The SPOTR platform analyses photographs taken inside and around properties, using machine learning to identify potential hazards including damp patches, mould growth, cracks and other structural concerns. The system then compiles these findings into a centralised dashboard, replacing the traditional reliance on multiple spreadsheets and databases.

For housing providers like Stonewater, which manages over 40,000 homes nationwide, this technology offers a practical solution to the challenge of regular property assessments. Under current industry standards, full stock condition surveys typically occur every few years, despite annual safety checks being conducted more frequently.

  • Automated risk identification from uploaded property photos
  • Centralised reporting platform for maintenance planning
  • Trained specifically on UK housing characteristics
  • Works alongside existing inspection regimes

Meeting Housing Standards Through Innovation

The adoption of AI technology comes as housing providers face increased scrutiny under the Social Housing Regulation Act 2023, the Decent Homes Standard and Awaab's Law. These regulations have placed greater emphasis on prompt identification and resolution of housing quality issues.

Stonewater's Director of Asset Strategy, Robert Panou, explained: "While our existing processes maintain safety standards, we recognised room for improvement. Our staff and contractors frequently visit properties, and whilst we can't train everyone to spot every potential risk, they can easily take photographs for the AI system to analyse."

The housing association spent a year collaborating with SPOTR to train the AI software specifically on UK property features, ensuring the system understands the unique characteristics of British homes. This tailored approach allows the technology to identify issues that might be missed during routine visits.

For homeowners and tenants, this development could mean faster identification of maintenance issues, potentially preventing minor problems from developing into more serious concerns. Housing providers might consider how similar technologies could complement their existing property management strategies whilst maintaining human oversight for complex cases.

As AI continues to develop, its applications in property maintenance could expand further, offering housing associations new tools to meet their obligations and improve living conditions for residents across the country.

item.title: Knight Frank reports summer surge in London sales market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London’s property market has bucked the traditional summer slowdown, with new figures revealing a notable surge in buyer activity across the capital. According to Knight Frank’s latest data, exchanges in the mainstream market rose by 15% between May and July compared to the same period last year, with July alone seeing a 34% annual increase. The figures suggest that committed buyers are driving momentum despite broader economic uncertainties.

Strong demand across key London boroughs

The uptick in transactions has been particularly pronounced in several sought-after areas, including Chelsea, Kensington, Notting Hill, Wandsworth, and Queen’s Park. Knight Frank attributes this to improved stock levels, giving buyers more options to find suitable properties. Accepted offers rose by 35% year-on-year over the three-month period, while new applicant numbers increased by 7%, indicating sustained interest in London’s housing market.

Andrew Groocock, COO of Knight Frank’s estate agency division, noted that needs-based buyers—such as those relocating, upsizing, or making lifestyle changes—are fuelling much of the activity. Unlike investors who may pause during uncertain times, these purchasers are pressing ahead with transactions, providing stability to the market.

Growing confidence in prime central London

The data also highlights renewed confidence in Prime Central London, where buyers are identifying value opportunities. While this segment had seen subdued activity in recent years, the current conditions appear to be encouraging more commitments. Groocock observed that purchasers are becoming increasingly decisive, particularly in areas where pricing has adjusted to reflect market conditions.

For homeowners considering a move, the current climate may present favourable timing, with competitive mortgage rates and a wider selection of available properties. However, as always, seeking independent financial advice before making significant decisions could be beneficial.

With demand holding steady and transaction volumes rising, London’s property market is demonstrating resilience—even during what is typically a quieter season. Whether this momentum continues into autumn remains to be seen, but for now, the capital’s housing market appears to be defying expectations.
